lesson.title: The Three Whens: wann, als, wenn
lesson.subtitle: English 'when' does three jobs — German hires three words, all verb-final

hook.title: The When-Split
hook.content: English when is one word doing shift work: the question (When do you come?), the once-only past (when I was a child), the repeater (when it rains). German refuses the overtime and hires three. wann asks the question — the twin of when, same ancient root. wenn takes the repeater AND the condition (if) — wann's etymological doublet, the same word split into two jobs. And als marks the once-only past — but here is the twist: als is NOT in the when-family at all. It is the twin of English also (all-so → 'as' → 'than'), the same als you drilled as 'than' in the comparison gym. English collapsed three words into one and one into three; German keeps the divisions sharp.

footnotes.title: The Doublet Test
footnotes.content: wann and wenn were one word in Old High German (hwanne) — exactly like English when, which comes from the same *hwan. wann kept the question job, wenn took the clause job. So when you hesitate between them, you are really choosing between 'asking' and 'linking' — the same choice English hides inside one spelling.

pattern.title: Three Jobs, Three Words, One Basement
pattern.content: wann — the question: Wann kommst du? And the indirect question: Ich weiß nicht, wann er kommt (verb-final — the basement rule fires). als — the once-only past: Als Kind war ich... (as/when I was a child — the war from the fortress pasts), Als ich gestern kam... — plus its old job, 'than': älter als du. wenn — the repeater and the condition: Wenn es regnet, lese ich (when(ever) it rains, I read — and if it rains, the same sentence). Every one of the three drops the verb to the clause end: wann er kommt, als ich kam, wenn ich Zeit habe. If you can already build weil-clauses, you can build all three.
pattern.linguist_note: als ← OHG alsō, al ('all') + sō ('so') — the exact formation of English also. 'Than' and 'as' both grew out of 'entirely so' by the same worn-road semantic route German still shows transparently.

exercises.prompt: The when-split — match each sentence with its reading:
exercises.target_answer: Wann kommst du, als ich ein Kind war, wenn es regnet lese ich, älter als du, als mein Freund kam, wenn der Lehrer kommt, wenn die Person geht
exercises.explanation: wann asks, als marks the unique past moment (and 'than'), wenn repeats and conditions.

exercises.meaning: Wann kommst du? = when are you coming?
exercises.explanation: Questions take wann — the exact twin of English when, keeping the question job.

exercises.prompt: '_____ ich gestern kam, war es spät.' (a one-time past moment):
exercises.meaning: Als ich gestern kam, war es spät = when I arrived yesterday, it was late
exercises.explanation: One specific past event → als. Repeating or future conditions → wenn. English 'when' covers both; German splits them.

exercises.prompt: wann and wenn are doublets of one ancient word. Which English word is their twin?
exercises.explanation: wann and wenn descend from the same word as English when: English kept one spelling, German split asking (wann) from linking (wenn).

exercises.prompt: Assemble the repeater: 'When it rains, I read'
exercises.meaning: Wenn es regnet, lese ich = when(ever) it rains, I read

vocab_hints.note: regnen — the rain-verb; es regnet = it rains

exercises.explanation: wenn builds the clause and the verb goes to the basement: regnet waits, lese waits — weil's rule, one more employee.

summary.outcome: Choose between wann, als and wenn correctly and build all three with verb-final order.

use_example.german: Wann kommst du? — Wenn es regnet, lese ich.
use_example.english: When are you coming? — When it rains, I read.

summary.takeaway: wann asks, als marks the once-only past (and 'than'), wenn repeats and conditions — and all three park the verb.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: ob — whether or not — the indirect yes/no word and English if's true twin.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from The Three Whens: wann, als, wenn (Wenn es regnet, lese ich = when(ever) it rains, I read):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wenn es regnet lese ich" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of The Three Whens: wann, als, wenn without relying on short-term echo.

wann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwan — the exact twin of English when. [wiktionary]

als.etymology_derivation: Kin to English else (both from the *alja- 'other' family) — the comparative particle. [wiktionary]

wenn.context_phrase: Wenn ich Zeit habe, lese ich.
wenn.context_translation: When(ever) I have time, I read.
wenn.etymology_derivation: Old High German hwanne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan — the exact twin of English when and the etymological doublet of German wann: wann asks the question, wenn builds the clause. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

regnen.context_translation: It is raining in Berlin today.
regnen.etymology_derivation: Denominal verb from Regen (rain, already known — the y→g twin of English rain). [wiktionary]

lesen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lesaną 'to gather' — cognate with archaic English lease 'to glean'; reading is gathering words. [wiktionary]

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

lehrer.context_phrase: Der Lehrer kommt in die Klasse.
lehrer.context_translation: The teacher comes into the class.
lehrer.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of lehren (teach) + -er; lehren is cognate with English learn/lore. [wiktionary]

person.context_translation: I do not know this person.
person.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German persōn, the same Latin loan as English person. [wiktionary]

freund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frijōndz, 'the loving one' — the exact twin of English friend. [wiktionary]

küste.etymology_derivation: From early modern Dutch kust, from Old French coste, from Latin costa, rib. English coast is the listed cognate from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

professor.context_phrase: Der Professor unterrichtet an der Universität.
professor.context_translation: The professor teaches at the university.
professor.etymology_derivation: A learned borrowing of Latin professor (one who declares publicly); English professor is the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

erwachsener.context_phrase: Nur Erwachsene zahlen den vollen Preis.
erwachsener.context_translation: Only adults pay the full price.
erwachsener.etymology_derivation: The nominalized adjective erwachsen, grown — the participle of wachsen, to grow, which the page lists as cognate with English wax, the old grow verb as in the waxing moon. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
